raw_case_text:
A 50 years-old male born in Morocco was admitted to the Hospital for detection of visceral PET positive lymph nodes. He was a former smoker (quit 5 years before admission; 31 pack years) and his occupation was working with plastic. He had been treated for his HIV infection for 5 years. Recently, he had been submitted to surgery and radiotherapy for rectal cancer. He had antibodies against surface Hepatitis B virus and was therefore also treated with Tenofovir, Lamivudine and Efavirenz.
Radiographic and Nuclear Investigations were previously carried out for a low-grade fever of unknown origin. Physical examination documented hepatosplenomegaly and enlarged lymph nodes in the inguinal area.
Altered routine blood tests results are reported in Table 1. Computed tomography scan of the thorax and abdomen mainly showed disseminated enlarged lymph nodes (mediastinum, abdomen) and an enlarged liver and spleen with splenic and portal veins showing enlarged diameters. (Figure 1)
The clinical reasoning was based on three pillars: 1; clinical profile characterized by low grade fever in an HIV patient already under retroviral treatment, 2; laboratory findings characterized by moderate white cells cytopenia (2.45 x 109/L), hypergammaglobulinemia (38.7%), an increase of erythrosedimentation rate (85 mm/h) and a mild increase of beta2-microglobulinemia (5.5 mg/L) and 3; imaging features, mainly represented by enlarged visceral PET positive lymph nodes. Therefore, the most probable diagnosis is included in the following differential diagnosis list: lymphoproliferative disorders, infections (fungal or parasite infections) and metastatic epithelial tumors. PET positive reachable lymph nodes are mainly sited in the mediastinum. Because the lymphoproliferative disorders in HIV positive patients are usually of the large B cell subtypes and a diagnosis is possible using cytological material and infections manifesting with visceral enlarged lymph nodes are more frequently due to intracellular microscopically or microbiologically easy to identify agents (i.e. Cryptococcus, mycobacteria) and because inguinal lymph nodes are frequently not specifically inflamed, a transesophageal ultrasound (EUS) approach was scheduled with fine needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB, 22 G needle) of lymph nodes in station 4L.
Smears and cell block preps stained by May Grunwald Giemsa, Papanicolaou, Hematoxylin-Eosin and Giemsa were analyzed. Histiocytes laden by amastigotes were identified; amastigotes were also found outside the cells (Figure 2). Amastigotes is one of the transformation stages (the intracellular phase) of the Leishmania parasites life cycle. It is the form the Leishmania parasite takes in the vertebrate host and it is diagnostic when found. A final diagnosis of Lehismaniasis was therefore done. A molecular test on peripheral blood confirmed the morphologic diagnosis. Leishmania donovani DNA copies were present (1,700 genome copies/mL). Other microbiological investigations (bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex type I and II viruses) were negative. The patient was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg iv for 5 days).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old male with HIV infection presented for evaluation of visceral PET-positive lymphadenopathy and low-grade fever of unknown origin.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient is a 50-year-old male with HIV on antiretroviral therapy who underwent radiographic and nuclear investigations for investigation of persistent low-grade fever of unknown origin. Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (PET) revealed hypermetabolic visceral lymph nodes, prompting admission for diagnostic evaluation of suspected lymphoproliferative disorder, opportunistic infection, or metastatic recurrence.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed 5 years prior; history of rectal adenocarcinoma treated with surgical resection and radiotherapy; presence of antibodies against surface hepatitis B virus. Former smoker (quit 5 years prior, 31 pack-years). Occupation: plastic manufacturing. Epidemiological background: born in Morocco.
subjective.review_of_systems: Low-grade fever of unknown origin. Home medications: tenofovir, lamivudine, efavirenz. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Abdominal examination documented hepatosplenomegaly. Lymphatic examination revealed enlarged lymph nodes in the inguinal region.
objective.routine_investigations: White blood cell count: 2.45 x 109/L (moderate leukopenia); Hypergammaglobulinemia: 38.7%; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 85 mm/h; Beta-2-microglobulin: 5.5 mg/L. Microbiological investigations: negative for bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and herpes simplex virus (HSV) types I and II.
objective.advanced_workup: Computed tomography (CT) of thorax and abdomen: disseminated enlarged lymph nodes involving mediastinum and abdomen; hepatosplenomegaly with dilated diameters of splenic and portal veins. Positron emission tomography (PET): visceral PET-positive hypermetabolic lymph nodes, predominantly in the mediastinum. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) with fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB, 22G needle) of station 4L mediastinal lymph nodes: smears and cell blocks stained with May-Grunwald-Giemsa, Papanicolaou, H&E, and Giemsa.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Visceral leishmaniasis (Leishmania donovani) presenting as hypermetabolic mediastinal and abdominal lymphadenopathy in an HIV-coinfected individual.
Diagnostic confirmation: Cytological examination of station 4L lymph node FNAB smears and cell block preps demonstrated histiocytes laden with amastigotes as well as extracellular amastigotes. Peripheral blood molecular PCR confirmed Leishmania donovani DNA with 1,700 genome copies/mL.
Differentials ruled out: Large B-cell lymphoma / lymphoproliferative disorders, metastatic recurrence of rectal adenocarcinoma, mycobacterial infection (tuberculosis), cryptococcal / fungal infection, CMV, and HSV.
Treatment and clinical course: Treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg IV daily for 5 days).
